content.rendered:
First check-in

Your first check-in with your mentee is an opportunity to learn more about their interests, their goals, and to get a sense of how best to work together. In this initial chat, it can help to cover the following:

Can you tell me about yourself?

  • Take this opportunity to learn a bit about your mentee’s background, while also sharing your own.
  • How did you become a mentorEvent Supporter Event Supporter (formerly Mentor) is someone who has already organised a WordCamp and has time to meet with their assigned mentee every 2 weeks, they talk over where they should be in their timeline, help them to identify their issues, and also identify solutions for their issues.?
  • What is your experience in the WordPress community?

What are your goals for participating in WordPress Credits?

  • Understanding your mentee’s goals for participating in WordPress Credits can help give you something to refer back to as they begin making decisions around their project.
  • Do they want to learn about open sourceOpen Source Open Source denotes software for which the original source code is made freely available and may be redistributed and modified. Open Source **must be** delivered via a licensing model, see GPL. more generally?
  • Is there a specific skillset they’re seeking to build on?
  • What makes them excited about the program?

Do you have any experience with WordPress or open source communities?

Learning about the student’s background with WordPress can help guide some initial conversations around navigating Learn WordPress, working through the WordPress user courses, and understanding any background information they have on WordPress tools and development.

Set expectations

  • The amount of time students have to complete the program varies per institution.
  • Work together with your student early on to figure out a sustainable pace that will allow them to meet any key deadlines, while also creating enough momentum to build on their contributions.

Set regular meeting times

  • Weekly meetings are an important part of building trust between you and your mentee, in addition to helping answer questions and keeping progress on track.
  • Set a time to meet weekly early on, so you can both make the most of the time you have available.

Day-1 Onboarding Checklist

Verify your mentee has a WordPress.orgWordPress.org The community site where WordPress code is created and shared by the users. This is where you can download the source code for WordPress core, plugins and themes as well as the central location for community conversations and organization. https://wordpress.org/ account, has joined the Make WordPress SlackSlack Slack is a Collaborative Group Chat Platform https://slack.com/. The WordPress community has its own Slack Channel at https://make.wordpress.org/chat/ workspace (#wpcredits), and can access the course on Learn WordPress.

Proactive unblocking

Encourage your mentee not to stay blocked: reassure them that if they are stuck on any lesson or setup for more than 30–45 minutes, they should reach out in #wpcredits or message you on Slack.

Agree on Week 1 next steps

Before wrapping up, confirm the mentee knows their immediate priorities: beginning the introductory Learn WordPress modules, saying hello in #wpcredits, and knowing how to log their hours.

At the end of the meeting, be sure to leave space for questions and follow-up, ideally on Slack, with any final tasks the student should focus on in their first week.

Week 2

Key progress indicators

  • Your student should actively be working through the WordPress Credits Course on Learn WordPress.
  • Slack accounts should be set up and active.
  • Hours logged for Week 1 should be confirmed and up to date.

Helpful questions or topics for the second meeting

  • How has your progress been in the WordPress Credits course? 
  • Do you have any questions about what you’ve learned?
  • Were you able to sign-up for Slack? Do you have any questions about how it works?
    • If they haven’t already, encourage them to introduce themselves in #wpcredits.
  • What are your goals for this week?
  • Note: If your mentee is finding it difficult to keep up with the course workload, suggest breaking lessons into smaller daily 30-minute blocks rather than cramming.

Week 3

Key progress indicators

  • Students should be moving through or finishing the WordPress Credits Course on Learn WordPress.
  • Hours logged should be consistent with the student’s steady progress through the program.

Helpful questions or topics for the third week

  • How is the WordPress Credits course? 
  • Do you have any questions about the lessons you’ve covered?
  • What WordPress user course(s) are you planning to complete?
  • Which Make WordPress teams (such as Documentation, Testing, or Polyglots) are catching your interest?
  • What are your goals for this week?
    • Note: It can be helpful to set a goal of setting up their project site at this point for this week or week 4.
    • Reassure your mentee that this only needs to be a simple, free WordPress blog for publishing weekly updates.

Week 4

Key progress indicators

  • Ideally, students should be completing or starting to complete the onboarding phase and moving into their project-based work.
  • Students should have set up or start setting up their project websites to begin publishing weekly updates.
    • Encourage your mentee to treat this site as a living portfolio to showcase their skills, problem-solving, and contributions to future employers, clients, or professors.

Helpful questions or topics for the fourth week

  • What were some takeaways from the WordPress User courses? 
  • Do you have any questions about where and how to use WordPress? Or how it works?
  • Have you set up your project site? If not, is there anything blocking you?
  • Which Make WordPress team(s) have you decided to contribute to, and have you joined their team Slack channel?
  • Encourage your mentee to publish their first introductory post on their project site and share the link with you.
  • Continue to set goals for the week, checking in with them about moving into the project phase of the program.

Weeks 5-12 (project-phase)

Depending on the student’s program, the timeline for the project phase may need to be adjusted. Consider this in your first few planning meetings.

Key progress indicators

  • Students should review and complete the contribution team information. 
  • Over the course of the following weeks, your mentee will decide on which team(s) they want to contribute and understand pathways for how to do so. 
  • As they begin to contribute, you should continue encouraging them to observe and/or participate in ongoing team meetings, projects, and other forms of engagement with the WordPress community.

Helpful questions or topics during the project phase

  • How were you able to find information on contributing?
  • Are there any places where you feel blocked or unsure of next steps?
  • Have you reviewed the areas of immediate contribution? Do any of those items sound like an interesting start?
  • This can also be a good moment to review project sites and presentations from previous students.
  • What is one small, bite-sized task or ticket we can target this week to get your first contribution landed?
  • Encourage a brief mid-week async check-in on Slack so your mentee never stays blocked between weekly calls.

Final week(s)

At the end of the project phase, students need to complete their wrap-up tasks, which include:

  • Presenting their project work, providing an overview of their progress and key learnings.
  • Attending a WordPress event, online or in person.
  • Publishing a final summary post on their project blog highlighting all their contributions, tickets, or translations.

Helpful questions or topics for these final check-ins:

  • Do you have any questions about attending a MeetupMeetup Meetup groups are locally-organized groups that get together for face-to-face events on a regular basis (commonly once a month). Learn more about Meetups in our Meetup Organizer Handbook.?
  • When you’re finished, don’t forget to complete the final lesson in the course to receive your certificate!

Questions/FAQ

What if my mentee can’t decide on a team to contribute to?

It’s understandable! There are a lot of ways to contribute to WordPress and it can be hard to know where your skills best fit in the beginning. This can be a great opportunity to discuss your mentee’s interests, experience level, and what they’d like to get from the program. Review the areas of immediate contribution together and identify one or two initial tasks they can handle. Sometimes, taking the first step is the hardest part.

There’s no local community near my mentee. How can they attend an event?

Fortunately, there are plenty of online events that students can attend. To help find them, encourage your mentee to visit https://events.wordpress.org and filterFilter Filters are one of the two types of Hooks https://codex.wordpress.org/Plugin_API/Hooks. They provide a way for functions to modify data of other functions. They are the counterpart to Actions. Unlike Actions, filters are meant to work in an isolated manner, and should never have side effects such as affecting global variables and output. for the Online Event Format.

title.rendered: How to Use the Student Report Card inside the WordPress Education Dashboard

content.rendered:
The WordPress Education Dashboard is where your place on the WordPress Credits Program lives once you became an active student: your details, your mentorEvent Supporter Event Supporter (formerly Mentor) is someone who has already organised a WordCamp and has time to meet with their assigned mentee every 2 weeks, they talk over where they should be in their timeline, help them to identify their issues, and also identify solutions for their issues., your calls and your course, all on one page instead of scattered across email threads and spreadsheets.

After being activated as a student in our WP Credits database, you receive an email with your login information.

Your WordPress Education Dashboard is at wordpresseducation.org. Sign in to open your Student Report Card, or set a new password if you have not signed in before or have forgotten yours.

Signing in for the first time

  • The program makes your account for you, so there is no sign-up form. Once your mentor and your course are assigned, an email from the WordPress Education Dashboard asks you to set your password.
  • The link in that email works for a limited time. If it has expired, or the email never came, go to the password reset page, enter the email address you registered with, and a new link arrives at that address. Look in your spam or junk folder too.
  • After your password, the site may ask for a code. It arrives by email, with Login confirmation code in its subject line, and works for fifteen minutes.
  • If no email arrives at all, your account may have a different address from the one you are checking. Write to the program's address and a program managerProgram Manager Program Managers (formerly Super Deputies) are Program Supporters who can perform extra tasks on WordCamp.org like creating new sites and publishing WordCamps to the schedule. will put it right.

Once you are signed in, the Student guide on the site covers everything on your page in more detail.

The page you land on after logging in is your Student Report Card. Nobody else sees yours — not other students, and not other mentorsEvent Supporter Event Supporter (formerly Mentor) is someone who has already organised a WordCamp and has time to meet with their assigned mentee every 2 weeks, they talk over where they should be in their timeline, help them to identify their issues, and also identify solutions for their issues.. Only your own mentor and the program managers can see your record.

What is on your Report Card

My profile

Your program details as the program records hold them: your track, your internship dates, your educational institution, your tutor and your contribution team.

Four of these are yours to change. Press Edit and you can update:

  • WordPress.orgWordPress.org The community site where WordPress code is created and shared by the users. This is where you can download the source code for WordPress core, plugins and themes as well as the central location for community conversations and organization. https://wordpress.org/ — your profile page, or just your username.
  • SlackSlack Slack is a Collaborative Group Chat Platform https://slack.com/. The WordPress community has its own Slack Channel at https://make.wordpress.org/chat/ — your display name in the Making WordPress Slack.
  • Contribution team — the team you are contributing to.
  • Personal website — the site you built on the program, if you have one.

Press Save and the change is written straight back to the program records, so you never have to ask anybody to update them for you. Everything else on that list is maintained by your institution or the program, so it is shown but not editable.

My mentor

Who your mentor is and how to reach them — their WordPress.org profile, their Slack handle and their website, where they have shared them.

My mentor call

Your upcoming calls, and the calendar you book them from. There is more on this below.

My course and report form

Two buttons: Open your course takes you to your course on Learn WordPress, and your report form opens already filled in with your record, so you are not retyping your own details every time you report your hours.

Resources

At the foot of the page: the students Slack channel, the Student guide in the handbook, and Need help? — a question box that answers from the WordPress documentation and shows you which pages it read. Beside it, Updates, where notices like this one appear.

Booking a call with your mentor

Your mentor publishes the hours they are free, and you pick from them. No email back and forth about what suits.

  1. Go to My mentor call on your Report Card.
  2. Check Show times in at the top of the calendar. Every time on the page is shown in the timezone chosen there, and it starts on the one your device reports — so if you are travelling, or the guess is wrong, set it before you pick.
  3. Pick a day with open slots, then a time. The calendar tells you how long the call is.
  4. Add a line about what you would like to discuss. It is optional, but it is how your mentor knows what to prepare — bring a link to whatever you are working on.
  5. Book it. You and your mentor both get an email with a calendar invite attached, so it lands in your calendar rather than only on this page.

A reminder goes out 24 hours before the call. If something comes up you can cancel from the same section, and the slot goes straight back on the calendar for somebody else.

A few things worth knowing: slots closer than your mentor’s shortest notice are not offered, your mentor sets how far ahead the calendar runs and how many upcoming calls you may hold at once, and if the month you are looking at is empty, try a later one. If your mentor has not published any hours yet, the section will say so — give them a nudge in Slack.

If something looks wrong

Your program details come from the program records, so if your dates, institution or tutor are not right, that is worth raising rather than working around — tell your mentor or ask in the students Slack channel. Everything on your Report Card is private to you, so nothing you correct there is on show to anybody else.

Welcome aboard, and enjoy the program.

title.rendered: Introduction Guide for WP Credits Students

content.rendered:
Welcome to  WordPress Credits!

This guide will walk you through what to expect when joining the program, how it works, and how you can make the most of your experience.

WordPress Credits is open to students from all our partner institutions. If you don’t see your school on the list, please reach out to a faculty member or your institution’s administration office and ask them to fill out the interest form.

As an alternative, you can fill this student interest form after reaching out to a faculty member or your institution’s administration office.

What is WordPress Credits?

WordPress Credits is an educational program of the  WordPress FoundationWordPress Foundation The WordPress Foundation is a charitable organization founded by Matt Mullenweg to further the mission of the WordPress open source project: to democratize publishing through Open Source, GPL software. Find more on wordpressfoundation.org.. It gives students the opportunity to practice their skills in a real, global, open-source environment. Over the course of  150 hours  (typically 13 to 18 weeks), you’ll contribute to WordPress projects, guided by an experienced mentorEvent Supporter Event Supporter (formerly Mentor) is someone who has already organised a WordCamp and has time to meet with their assigned mentee every 2 weeks, they talk over where they should be in their timeline, help them to identify their issues, and also identify solutions for their issues., while learning how to collaborate in a distributed team.

WordPress Credits is open to students

What to Expect

  • Mentorship
    You’ll be paired with a mentor who will guide you throughout the program. MentorsEvent Supporter Event Supporter (formerly Mentor) is someone who has already organised a WordCamp and has time to meet with their assigned mentee every 2 weeks, they talk over where they should be in their timeline, help them to identify their issues, and also identify solutions for their issues. will meet with you once per week and provide asynchronous support (via SlackSlack Slack is a Collaborative Group Chat Platform https://slack.com/. The WordPress community has its own Slack Channel at https://make.wordpress.org/chat/ or other communication channels).
  • Time Commitment
    The program requires at least  150 hours (flexible to meet each institution’s needs). This usually means about  8–12 hours per week, depending on the program length (13–18 weeks). You can spread your hours flexibly, but you are expected to stay consistent. The program includes a theoretical onboarding phase and hands-on, practical activities.
  • Projects
    You’ll design and carry out a contribution project aligned with your studies and interests. Projects can involve many areas of WordPress, from community and events, to education, documentation, accessibilityAccessibility Accessibility (commonly shortened to a11y) refers to the design of products, devices, services, or environments for people with disabilities. The concept of accessible design ensures both “direct access” (i.e. unassisted) and “indirect access” meaning compatibility with a person’s assistive technology (for example, computer screen readers). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessibility), and more.
  • Community Involvement
    You’ll join the  WordPress.org Slack, attend team meetings when possible, and interact with global contributors. This is a chance to build connections and learn how an open-source community works.
  • Deliverables
    • Weekly updates on your project (usually published on your personal WordPress site)
    • A final presentation and wrap-up post about your journey and outcomes
    • Contribution credits in the WordPress ecosystem

What we mean by contributing to WordPress

Contributing to WordPress means taking part in a global open-source project where everyone can play a role. It is not limited to writing code: there are many ways to contribute based on individual interests and abilities.

Through the WordPress Credits program, you will discover that contribution is about engaging with the official teams that support the project. For example:

  • CoreCore Core is the set of software required to run WordPress. The Core Development Team builds WordPress.  team develop and maintain the WordPress software itself, improving performance, fixing bugs, and introducing new features that keep the platform stable and modern.
  • Polyglots  work on translations, making WordPress available in different languages.
  • Documentation  team review and improve guides, ensuring instructions remain accurate and clear.
  • Support  team answer questions in the forums, helping users solve problems.
  • Community  team organize local events and meetupsMeetup Meetup groups are locally-organized groups that get together for face-to-face events on a regular basis (commonly once a month). Learn more about Meetups in our Meetup Organizer Handbook., showing how collaboration helps projects grow. That’s the team behind the WordPress Credits project.
  • Training  create learning materials for learn.wordpress.orgWordPress.org The community site where WordPress code is created and shared by the users. This is where you can download the source code for WordPress core, plugins and themes as well as the central location for community conversations and organization. https://wordpress.org/, turning knowledge into shared resources.

These activities are essential to WordPress. By contributing, you will learn to collaborate with people from different backgrounds, practice communication, and understand how projects are organized on a global scale.

Contributing does not require building a pluginPlugin A plugin is a piece of software containing a group of functions that can be added to a WordPress website. They can extend functionality or add new features to your WordPress websites. WordPress plugins are written in the PHP programming language and integrate seamlessly with WordPress. These can be free in the WordPress.org Plugin Directory https://wordpress.org/plugins/ or can be cost-based plugin from a third-party. or fixing code. It means choosing a team, learning how it works, and dedicating time to support its goals. This is a practical way to gain experience and develop skills that are useful both inside and outside the WordPress community.

Immediate Contribution Opportunities

The WordPress project thrives on contributions from people all over the world. With WPCredits, we aim to guide you towards meaningful and accessible ways to get involved in the WordPress ecosystem. These are some of the immediate contribution areas where you can start your journey:

Build

For developers and tinkerers who want to write code, build tools, or improve existing projects.

Design

For designers, photographers, and anyone with an eye for how things look and work.

Write

For writers and editors who want to improve documentation, create guides, or develop learning content.

Test

For detail-oriented people who want to find bugs, verify fixes, or review guides.

Translate

For multilingual contributors who want to make WordPress accessible in more languages.

Organize

For people who like coordinating, triaging, and keeping things running smoothly.

Promote

For communicators who want to help spread the word and support community events.

Your Responsibilities

  • Dedicate the required time and stay consistent with your contributions
  • Communicate proactively with your mentor and team members
  • Share progress updates regularly
  • Respect the community’s  Code of Conduct
  • Approach challenges with curiosity, responsibility, and openness

What You’ll Gain

By the end of the program, you will:

  • Gain hands-on experience in  open-source collaboration
  • Build  technical and professional skills  like project management, communication, problem solving, and teamwork
  • Connect with mentors, peers, and professionals in the WordPress ecosystem
  • Create a portfolio of contributions you can showcase in your career path

Inside the Course

Next Steps

Once your institution has signed a partnership with the WordPress Foundation, you can enrol in the program by following the next steps:

  1. Apply  using the application form that your institution shared with you.
  2. Once selected, you’ll receive the instructions to set up your student account.
  3. Connect with your mentor and complete the onboarding phase.
  4. Start contributing and building your project!

If you don’t see your school among our partner institutions, please reach out to a faculty member or your administration office and invite them to fill out our Institution Interest Form so we can explore a partnership together.

As an alternative, you can fill this student interest form after reaching out to a faculty member or your institution’s administration office.

Remember

This program is not just about completing hours. It’s about  learning, growing, and contributing meaningfully. Take initiative, stay engaged, and use this opportunity to connect your studies with real-world practice.

We’re excited to have you join the program and can’t wait to see what you’ll create!

If you have any questions before applying, please send us an email at  the program's address.

Course link that the student will take – https://learn.wordpress.org/course/wordpress-credits/ 

BEFORE THE PROJECT STARTS (Onboarding phase)

  • Set up a call with the student to introduce and get started. You can schedule a group call as well if they understand the same language.

Get the student set up

  • Confirm they’ve created their WordPress.orgWordPress.org The community site where WordPress code is created and shared by the users. This is where you can download the source code for WordPress core, plugins and themes as well as the central location for community conversations and organization. https://wordpress.org/ profile.
  • Confirm they’ve joined the global WordPress SlackSlack Slack is a Collaborative Group Chat Platform https://slack.com/. The WordPress community has its own Slack Channel at https://make.wordpress.org/chat/ (and their local/regional Slack, if one exists for their language/area).
  • Make sure they know the key channels: #wpcredits (general) and where to reach you.
  • Create a Slack DM group, MentorEvent Supporter Event Supporter (formerly Mentor) is someone who has already organised a WordCamp and has time to meet with their assigned mentee every 2 weeks, they talk over where they should be in their timeline, help them to identify their issues, and also identify solutions for their issues. <> Mentee, for regular check-ins.
  • Send/confirm they have their individual tracking/form link (usually shared in their Welcome email; you can also pull it from your Airtable dashboard if they lose it).

Confirm foundational courses are completed

  • Open sourceOpen Source Open Source denotes software for which the original source code is made freely available and may be redistributed and modified. Open Source **must be** delivered via a licensing model, see GPL. basics and WordPress.
  • Differences between WordPress.comWordPress.com An online implementation of WordPress code that lets you immediately access a new WordPress environment to publish your content. WordPress.com is a private company owned by Automattic that hosts the largest multisite in the world. This is arguably the best place to start blogging if you have never touched WordPress before. https://wordpress.com/ and .org.
  • How decisions are made in the WordPress project.
  • Beginner / Intermediate / Advanced WordPress User course(s): 1 to 3, depending on their existing skill level.

Help them choose a real contribution project

  • Walk them through the list of teams (CoreCore Core is the set of software required to run WordPress. The Core Development Team builds WordPress., Polyglots, Support, Documentation, Test, Playground, Community, Training, TV, Photos, Design, Themes, DEIB, AccessibilityAccessibility Accessibility (commonly shortened to a11y) refers to the design of products, devices, services, or environments for people with disabilities. The concept of accessible design ensures both “direct access” (i.e. unassisted) and “indirect access” meaning compatibility with a person’s assistive technology (for example, computer screen readers). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessibility), MetaMeta Meta is a term that refers to the inside workings of a group. For us, this is the team that works on internal WordPress sites like WordCamp Central and Make WordPress., Hosting) and point them to make.wordpress.org/[team-name] for each.
  • Double-check the project idea against what qualifies: it should tie to a team’s real goals, produce something useful to the wider community, and involve collaboration, not be a personal blog/portfolio or disconnected one-off experiment.
  • If relevant, share hosting/pluginPlugin A plugin is a piece of software containing a group of functions that can be added to a WordPress website. They can extend functionality or add new features to your WordPress websites. WordPress plugins are written in the PHP programming language and integrate seamlessly with WordPress. These can be free in the WordPress.org Plugin Directory https://wordpress.org/plugins/ or can be cost-based plugin from a third-party. discount codes for their personal website (these come from the program, not the course itself).

Set expectations early

  • Explain the weekly meeting rhythm and 24-hour async response expectation.
  • Review the Code of ConductCode of Conduct “A code of conduct is a set of rules outlining the norms, rules, and responsibilities or proper practices of an individual party.” - Wikipedia with them.
  • Make sure they understand lessons unlock sequentially, and they must submit their tracking form after each one.

DURING THE PROJECT (active contribution phase)

Weekly rhythm

  • Hold a ~30-min weekly meeting (same day/time) or a group meeting if several students share a language.
  • Cover: progress since last check-in, blockers/questions, goals for next week, feedback and encouragement.
  • Respond to Slack/email within 24 hours on working days, even if just to confirm receipt and give a timeframe.

Tracking and verification

  • Check their Airtable submissions before each weekly meeting.
  • Verify their website/posts are genuine updates and reflections on the contribution work (not off-topic content).
  • Verify Slack participation and any event attendance links they’ve shared.
  • If something doesn’t fit the course’s purpose, ask them to revise it via their tracking link.

Reporting

  • Post a short biweekly update in #wpcredits-private summarizing each student’s status.
  • Escalate immediately (don’t wait for the biweekly cycle) if there’s an urgent issue.

Troubleshooting as it comes up

  • Not engaging: reach out proactively, simplify tasks; escalate to the program's address if there’s no response after 4+ attempts over 2+ weeks.
  • Overwhelmed/behind: help reprioritize, set mini-deadlines, celebrate small wins.
  • Wants to change project scope: understand why, connect them to the right team, check feasibility, have them keep (not discard) earlier work.
  • Technical/workflow blockers: point to Slack/forums/docs, give a quick demo, encourage documenting the fix.

Closing out

  • Confirm their final reflection post is published (Wrap-up stage).
  • Ask them to fill out the feedback forms using the correct email (the same one they have in the personal link, without spelling errors and without capital letters).
  • Point them toward ongoing resources if they want to stay involved (Learn WordPress, Make WordPress, WordPress.tv, WordPress Education).

If you are a collaborating institution or sponsor, please find WordPress Credits logos here to insert in your dedicated page about your collaboration with the WordPress Credits program.

WordPress Credits – Horizontal LogoDownload
WordPress Credits – Vertical LogoDownload
WordPress Credits – Isolated LogoDownload

Help guide the next generation of contributors in WordPress Credits, a flagship educational program of the WordPress FoundationWordPress Foundation The WordPress Foundation is a charitable organization founded by Matt Mullenweg to further the mission of the WordPress open source project: to democratize publishing through Open Source, GPL software. Find more on wordpressfoundation.org..

WordPress Credits connects university students with real-world, open-source contribution opportunities. Over 150+ hours, students learn how to collaborate in distributed teams, work on meaningful projects, and gain valuable skills that bridge academia and professional pathways.

Learn more about the program and the mentorEvent Supporter Event Supporter (formerly Mentor) is someone who has already organised a WordCamp and has time to meet with their assigned mentee every 2 weeks, they talk over where they should be in their timeline, help them to identify their issues, and also identify solutions for their issues. role: WordPress Credits Handbook and Mentor Guide.

Mentor Requirements

  • Minimum 2 hours per week available for the entire duration of the program (current cohorts last 13 to 18 weeks but it may vary)
  • Availability to sync once a week with students
  • Ability to provide asynchronous support (SlackSlack Slack is a Collaborative Group Chat Platform https://slack.com/. The WordPress community has its own Slack Channel at https://make.wordpress.org/chat/, email, or other tools)
  • Commitment to provide a meaningful mentorship experience

Mentor Responsibilities

  • Guide up to 5 students per mentor (if you have more availability, let us know — we may assign additional students)
  • Support students in understanding contribution tasks and navigating the WordPress community
  • Encourage collaboration, accountability, and skill growth
  • Provide feedback on student progress and final projects

Additional Information

  • MentorsEvent Supporter Event Supporter (formerly Mentor) is someone who has already organised a WordCamp and has time to meet with their assigned mentee every 2 weeks, they talk over where they should be in their timeline, help them to identify their issues, and also identify solutions for their issues. will be vetted before selection. You will receive an acceptance or rejection email after review.
  • Currently, we are onboarding students from a limited number of institutions. However, we want to prepare a pool of mentors worldwide so we can match you with students as soon as more universities join the program.
  • Your mentorship will help students connect their academic learning to real-world practice, while shaping the next wave of WordPress contributors.

Ultimately, being a great mentor in the WP Credits program means embracing the role of a teacher. It’s about more than just providing answers; it’s about fostering understanding, encouraging problem-solving, and nurturing a student’s professional growth. Your patience, clarity, and active investment in their journey will be the most significant factors in their success, and the success of the entire program.

Eligibility Criteria

To join the WP Credits mentor group, candidates should:

  • Have a wp.org account that shows both their wp.org and slack names (if not, it means they are not in slack with that wp.org account). 
  • Demonstrate alignment with the WordPress Foundation mission and values, including openness, collaboration, and respect.
  • Show a positive and supportive attitude, being a good communicator and de-escalator in challenging situations.
  • Be committed to student success, willing to dedicate at least 2 hours per week for mentoring and guidance.
  • Have basic familiarity with the WordPress project, its community spaces, and contribution practices (long-term experience is not required, we will provide additional training according to each case).

Welcome to the WP Credits mentorship program! Your role is crucial, you’re not just a guide but a catalyst for the next generation of WordPress contributors. Based on firsthand experience, here are some key insights and practical tips to help you excel and make a lasting impact.

1. The Power of Consistent Communication

  • The Challenge: Students can feel isolated or lose momentum without regular check-ins. Asynchronous communication (like emails or messages) is essential, but it’s often not enough to build rapport and address complex issues.
  • The Tip: Schedule a Weekly Call. Make it a non-negotiable part of your routine. This dedicated time serves multiple purposes:
  • Builds Trust: A regular voice or video call creates a stronger personal connection than text alone.
  • Solves Blockers Quickly: It’s the perfect forum for students to ask questions that are difficult to articulate in writing. You can use screen-sharing to troubleshoot problems in real-time.
  • Maintains Momentum: Knowing there’s a weekly touchpoint keeps students accountable and motivated to progress on their tasks.

2. Setting Clear Expectations from Day One

  • The Challenge: Ambiguity is the enemy of progress. Students may be new to open-source workflows, project management tools, or the specific tasks they’re assigned. Unclear instructions lead to confusion, delays, and frustration.
  • The Tip: Over-Explain and Document.
  • Break It Down: Don’t just assign a task; explain why it’s important, what the final outcome should look like, and where to find resources.
  • Define “Done”: Clearly outline the criteria for a task to be considered complete. Does it need a code review? A pull request? A published post?
  • Provide Examples: Share links to exemplary tickets, well-written commit messages, or past student work. A good example is worth a thousand words.

3. Unlocking Potential by Understanding Aptitudes

  • The Challenge: Students have diverse backgrounds, skills, and learning paces. A one-size-fits-all approach can leave some bored and others overwhelmed.
  • The Tip: Be a Detective and a Coach.
  • Assess Early: In your first calls, ask about their previous experience with coding, design, writing, or project management. Give them small, varied tasks to see what they enjoy and excel at.
  • Play to Their Strengths: Once you identify a student’s aptitude (e.g., front-end development, documentation, QA testing), you can tailor tasks to fit their skills and interests, which dramatically increases engagement and quality of work.
  • Challenge Them Appropriately: The goal is growth. Assign tasks that stretch their abilities without breaking their confidence.

4. Mastering the Art of Time Management

  • The Challenge: Students juggle multiple commitments. It’s easy for them to underestimate a task’s complexity or procrastinate, risking project deadlines.
  • The Tip: Be a Proactive Timekeeper.
  • Estimate Together: When assigning a task, ask the student to estimate how long they think it will take. Compare it with your own estimate and discuss any discrepancies. This teaches them valuable project scoping skills.
  • Set Mini-Deadlines: Break larger tasks into smaller, manageable chunks with their own due dates. This makes progress more measurable and prevents last-minute rushes.
  • Check In Between Calls: A simple mid-week message (“How is task X going? Any blockers?”) shows you’re engaged and helps you identify time-related issues early.
  • In Summary: Embrace the Teacher Mindset

Welcome! WordPress Credits is an experiential learning initiative designed to bridge the gap between academic theory and real-world digital contribution. By joining this program, your institution empowers students to become active participants in the open-source ecosystem while building a verifiable professional portfolio.

Flexible ways to integrate WordPress Credits

Each institution decides how the program fits its academic structure. The most common approaches are:

  • As an internship – students complete supervised hours that count toward an internship or work-placement requirement.
  • As an embedded module – integrate the program, or selected courses from it, into an existing subject.
  • As a pre-graduation project – use it as the practical or capstone project students complete before finishing their studies.
  • As an elective or extracurricular credit – offer it as a standalone elective.

These are the most common models, not the only ones. We’re happy to discuss any arrangement that works for your institution – our goal is for the time and work students invest to be formally recognized by their school or university.

Choosing your start date

There are no fixed global cohort dates. The program runs on your academic calendar: you choose start and end dates that fit your term, and students are enrolled with those dates.

Students enroll themselves (most cohorts)

Give students a clear internal deadline to complete the form – we ask that all responses are in at least 4 weeks before your start date, so accounts can be created and mentors paired before onboarding begins.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a limit to the number of students per cohort?
No fixed limit. Each mentor usually guides up to five students, so your cohort size depends on mentor availability at your chosen start date. Please share expected numbers at the consultation call.

How early do you need the full student list?
At least 4 weeks before your start date, so there is time to schedule a group onboarding calls mentors can be paired before onboarding begins.

Do we get access to a system to follow student progress?
Yes. Each institution has its own Institution Dashboard on the Education Directory, described in the Institution guide. Both ask you to sign in. You can also follow progress through students’ weekly published updates and their public WordPress.org contribution records.

When is the next start date?
Whenever suits your calendar. Institutions set their own start and end dates within their academic term, subject to the lead times above.

Does it cost anything?
No. The program, the learning platform, mentor training, and access to tools and resources are provided at no cost to the institution.

Who mentors our students?
Mentors are experienced contributors from the WordPress community. Faculty can also train as mentors and guide their own students.

Can students continue contributing after the program ends?
Yes. Many do, and their WordPress.org profile continues to record their contributions. We encourage students to remain active in the WordPress Ecosystem, so they can strengthen and build skills while contributing to a global open source project, connecting with professionals and companies worldwide.

  • Creating multilingual subtitles for educational videos
  • Writing or editing content
  • Assisting with community event organization
  • Developing training materials for Learn WordPress
  • Contributing code or performing testing
  • Supporting product development or design
  • Creating open source tools

3. Wrap-up

Students complete the program with a final reflection and evaluation.

  • Prepare and deliver a final presentation (remote or in person)
  • Submit feedback to help improve the program
  • Ensure their project and site are complete and publicly accessible

Mentorship and Support

Each student is paired with a mentor. A dedicated WordPress Foundation contact ensures alignment with program goals and academic requirements. Mentorship includes guidance, feedback, and regular check-ins.

Tracking Your Progress

All students track time spent on each task and project activity. This data helps the WordPress Foundation improve the program and report on its impact.

Why It Matters

WordPress Credits lowers the barriers to open source contribution, supports the academic and professional development of students, and helps build a diverse, sustainable contributor pipeline for the WordPress project.

By welcoming students, mentors, sponsors, and volunteers into this initiative, we are shaping not only the future of WordPress, but the future of open source itself.
